questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Fundamental Theorem of Line Integrals Over Parametric Curves
questions.problem: Let $f(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+y\operatorname{cos}⁡z.$ Given that $C$ is the path along the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,t,2t⟩$ for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}],$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

In our case, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,0,0⟩ \\ r(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨1,\frac{\pi }{2},\pi ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,0,0)$ and $(1,\frac{\pi }{2},\pi ).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(\pi ))-f(r(0)) \\  & =f(1,\frac{\pi }{2},\pi )-f(0,0,0) \\  & =(1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi )-(0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡0+0\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =(1+\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot (-1))-0 \\  & =1-\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}z+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y.$ Given that $C$ is the path along the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t,t⟩$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ],$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

In our case, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨1,0,0⟩ \\ r(2\pi ) & =⟨1,0,2\pi ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(1,0,0)$ and $(1,0,2\pi ).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(2\pi ))-f(r(0)) \\  & =f(1,0,2\pi )-f(1,0,0) \\  & =({1}^{2}\cdot 2\pi +1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡0)-({1}^{2}\cdot 0+1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =(2\pi +0)-0 \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Fundamental Theorem of Line Integrals When the Potential Function Is Not Given
questions.problem:
Consider the curve $C,$ defined parametrically as

$$
r(t)=⟨t,{e}^{t}⟩,\,0\le t\le 1.
$$

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ for $F=(3{x}^{2}{y}^{3}+2x)\,i+(3{x}^{3}{y}^{2}-4y)\,j.$ 

*Hint: You may wish to use the fact that $F$ is conservative.*
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

To apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we must first find a potential function $f$ such that $F=∇f.$ Since we're given that $F$ is conservative, we know that such a function exists. Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =3{x}^{2}{y}^{3}+2x, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =3{x}^{3}{y}^{2}-4y.\end{aligned}
$$

Reconstructing the function $f$ from its gradient in the usual way, we get

$$
f(x,y)={x}^{3}{y}^{3}+{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}.
$$

Note that we set $C=0$ for the arbitrary constant since we can use any function $f$ that satisfies $∇f=F.$

We're now ready to apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals. The position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,1⟩, \\ r(1) & =⟨1,e⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,1)$ and $(1,e).$

Finally, applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =f(1,e)-f(0,1) \\  & =({1}^{3}\cdot {e}^{3}+{1}^{2}-2\cdot {e}^{2})-({0}^{3}\cdot {1}^{3}+{0}^{2}-2\cdot {1}^{2}) \\  & ={e}^{3}+1-2{e}^{2}+2 \\  & ={e}^{3}-2{e}^{2}+3.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the curve $C,$ defined parametrically as

$$
r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+1,t⟩,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ for $F={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,i-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j.$ 

*Hint: You may wish to use the fact that $F$ is conservative.*
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

To apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we must first find a potential function $f$ such that $F=∇f.$ Since we're given that $F$ is conservative, we know that such a function exists. Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Reconstructing the function $f$ from its gradient in the usual way, we get

$$
f(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y.
$$

Note that we set $C=0$ for the arbitrary constant since we can use any function $f$ that satisfies $∇f=F.$

We're now ready to apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals. The position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨1,0⟩, \\ r(2\pi ) & =⟨4{\pi }^{2}+1,2\pi ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(1,0)$ and $(4{\pi }^{2}+1,2\pi ).$

Finally, applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =f(4{\pi }^{2}+1,2\pi )-f(1,0) \\  & ={e}^{4{\pi }^{2}+1}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi -{e}^{1}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & ={e}^{4{\pi }^{2}+1}-e \\  & =e({e}^{4{\pi }^{2}}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Fundamental Theorem of Line Integrals Over Cartesian Curves
questions.problem: Let $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y+1}.$ Given that $C$ is the path along the curve $y={e}^{x}+1$ for $x\in [0,\operatorname{ln}⁡2],$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

We start by parametrizing the curve $C.$ A suitable parametrization is

$$
r(t)=⟨t,{e}^{t}+1⟩,\,t\in [0,\operatorname{ln}⁡2].
$$

Then, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,2⟩, \\ r(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡2,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,2)$ and $(\operatorname{ln}⁡2,3).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(\operatorname{ln}⁡2))-f(r(0)) \\  & =f(\operatorname{ln}⁡2,3)-f(0,2) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2\cdot {e}^{3+1}-0\cdot {e}^{2+1} \\  & ={e}^{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$
